claims.source: The reduced affiliative engagement by subordinates was driven by a change in behaviour towards the simulated aggressor specifically: subordinates engaged in significantly less grooming with the simulated aggressor on conflict evenings compared to control evenings (proportion of time: Z = 2.521, N = 8, p = 0.008; Figure 5a; proportion of subordinates: Z = 2.201, N = 8, p = 0.033; Figure 5c), but there was no such treatment difference in the grooming of subordinates with the dominant whose calls were not played back (proportion of time: Z = 0.105, N = 8, p = 1; Figure 5b; proportion of subordinates: Z = 0.813, N = 8, p = 0.499; Figure 5d).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 5d.

claims.claim: Subordinate–subordinate grooming bouts were, on average, significantly longer on conflict evenings compared to control evenings (Z = 2.366, N = 7, p = 0.015).
claims.source: When considering all bouts between subordinate group members, there was no significant treatment difference in the proportion of time spent grooming (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: Z = 1.540, N = 8, p = 0.146), but subordinate–subordinate grooming bouts were, on average, significantly longer on conflict evenings compared to control evenings (Z = 2.366, N = 7, p = 0.015; Figure 6a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 6a.

claims.claim: There was no significant treatment difference in the proportion of time spent grooming between subordinate group members (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: Z = 1.540, N = 8, p = 0.146).
claims.source: When considering all bouts between subordinate group members, there was no significant treatment difference in the proportion of time spent grooming (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: Z = 1.540, N = 8, p = 0.146), but subordinate–subordinate grooming bouts were, on average, significantly longer on conflict evenings compared to control evenings (Z = 2.366, N = 7, p = 0.015; Figure 6a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The increase in the average duration of later subordinate–subordinate grooming is in line with the increase in bystander–bystander grooming seen in some species in the immediate aftermath of a contest.
claims.source: The increase in the average duration of later subordinate–subordinate grooming is in line with the increase in bystander–bystander grooming seen in some species in the immediate aftermath of a contest (Judge and Mullen, 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim compares the current findings to previous literature.

claims.claim: Bystander-bystander affiliation could reduce the group-wide social anxiety induced by aggression.
claims.source: Such affiliation could reduce the group-wide social anxiety induced by aggression (De Marco et al., 2010; Judge and Bachmann, 2013; Schino and Sciarretta, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about function supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The later reduction in grooming of aggressors by bystanders is the first evidence for a change in this direction.
claims.source: The later reduction in grooming of aggressors by bystanders is, to our knowledge, the first evidence for a change in this direction; some previous studies have documented increased grooming of aggressors by bystanders in the immediate aftermath of a single contest (Cordoni and Palagi, 2015; Palagi et al., 2008; Pallante et al., 2018), whilst a few others have found no evidence for such an increase (Judge, 1991; Romero et al., 2008; Verbeek and de Waal, 1997).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on comparison to previous literature.

claims.claim: Some previous studies have documented increased grooming of aggressors by bystanders in the immediate aftermath of a single contest.
claims.source: The later reduction in grooming of aggressors by bystanders is, to our knowledge, the first evidence for a change in this direction; some previous studies have documented increased grooming of aggressors by bystanders in the immediate aftermath of a single contest (Cordoni and Palagi, 2015; Palagi et al., 2008; Pallante et al., 2018), whilst a few others have found no evidence for such an increase (Judge, 1991; Romero et al., 2008; Verbeek and de Waal, 1997).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Some studies have found no evidence for increased grooming of aggressors by bystanders in the immediate aftermath of a contest.
claims.source: The later reduction in grooming of aggressors by bystanders is, to our knowledge, the first evidence for a change in this direction; some previous studies have documented increased grooming of aggressors by bystanders in the immediate aftermath of a single contest (Cordoni and Palagi, 2015; Palagi et al., 2008; Pallante et al., 2018), whilst a few others have found no evidence for such an increase (Judge, 1991; Romero et al., 2008; Verbeek and de Waal, 1997).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Subordinate bystanders could be avoiding the aggressor to reduce the likelihood of redirected aggression.
claims.source: Subordinate bystanders could be avoiding the aggressor to reduce the likelihood of redirected aggression, which parallels the main strategy employed in the immediate aftermath of contests by meerkat (Suricata suricatta) and rook (Corvus frugilegus) targets attempting to avoid renewed aggression (Benkada et al., 2020; Kutsukake and Clutton-Brock, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results supported by citations to similar behavior in other species.

claims.claim: Meerkat and rook targets employ avoidance as the main strategy in the immediate aftermath of contests to avoid renewed aggression.
claims.source: Subordinate bystanders could be avoiding the aggressor to reduce the likelihood of redirected aggression, which parallels the main strategy employed in the immediate aftermath of contests by meerkat (Suricata suricatta) and rook (Corvus frugilegus) targets attempting to avoid renewed aggression (Benkada et al., 2020; Kutsukake and Clutton-Brock, 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Within-group conflict can affect interactions beyond those between the protagonists.
claims.source: Our results support previous research showing that within-group conflict can affect interactions beyond those between the protagonists and highlight that bystanders can employ different conflict-management strategies depending on the identity of the group members involved.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current results and previous literature.

claims.claim: Bystanders can employ different conflict-management strategies depending on the identity of the group members involved.
claims.source: Our results support previous research showing that within-group conflict can affect interactions beyond those between the protagonists and highlight that bystanders can employ different conflict-management strategies depending on the identity of the group members involved.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential responses to simulated aggressors versus non-playback dominants.

claims.claim: Disagreements between two individuals can have wide-reaching and varied implications for affiliative behaviour, which underpins dyadic relationships and social structure in dwarf mongooses and many other group-living species.
claims.source: Disagreements between two individuals can thus have wide-reaching and varied implications for affiliative behaviour, which underpins dyadic relationships and social structure in dwarf mongooses (Kern and Radford, 2021; Kern and Radford, 2018) and many other group-living species (Cameron et al., 2009; Radford and Du Plessis, 2006; Silk et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is a general conclusion supported by the current results and citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Individuals can retain information relating to earlier within-group conflict and use it when making later decisions about management-related behaviours.
claims.source: The changes in evening grooming patterns once the group had moved from their afternoon foraging areas demonstrate that individuals can retain information relating to earlier within-group conflict and use it when making later decisions about management-related behaviours.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the delayed grooming effects observed in Experiment 2.

claims.claim: The specific reduction in grooming of perceived aggressors and not of non-playback dominants suggests decision-making about which groupmates to groom rather than a general byproduct of an altered physiological state.
claims.source: It is possible that hearing foraging displacements generates stress in bystanders, which could still be elevated on arrival at the sleeping burrow. But the specific reduction in grooming of perceived aggressors and not of non-playback dominants suggests decision-making about which groupmates to groom rather than a general byproduct of an altered physiological state.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential grooming patterns observed.

claims.claim: By using call playbacks, the delayed grooming effects are most likely driven by subordinate bystanders behaving differently towards perceived protagonists, rather than solicitation or rejection of grooming by the latter.
claims.source: Moreover, the use of playback simulations, rather than generation of actual contests, means that the delayed grooming effects are most likely driven by subordinate bystanders behaving differently towards perceived protagonists, rather than solicitation or rejection of grooming by the latter.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism based on the experimental design.

claims.claim: Dwarf mongooses can use vocal information to detect earlier cooperative contributions by groupmates and then reward them later.
claims.source: Previous work has shown that dwarf mongooses can use vocal information to detect earlier cooperative contributions by groupmates and then reward them later (Kern and Radford, 2018); we now provide experimental evidence for delayed post-conflict management behaviour.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Mongooses and many other social species are constantly monitoring the behaviour and interactions of groupmates, and are using memories of what they learn to inform later decisions.
claims.source: It is thus increasingly apparent that mongooses, as well as many other social species, are constantly monitoring the behaviour and interactions of groupmates, and are using memories of what they learn to inform later decisions (Tibbetts et al., 2020; Wittig et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a general conclusion supported by the current results and citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The cognitive demands of tracking individuals and their behaviours, remembering that information, and using it when making decisions explain why social interactions within and between groups are believed to be strong drivers of animal intelligence.
claims.source: The cognitive demands of tracking individuals and their behaviours, remembering that information, and using it when making decisions explain why social interactions within (Dunbar and Shultz, 2007) and between (Ashton et al., 2020) groups are believed to be strong drivers of animal intelligence.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on the social intelligence hypothesis.

claims.claim: Dwarf mongooses can extract information about within-group conflicts, and the identity of at least some protagonists, from vocal cues alone.
claims.source: Our experiments show that dwarf mongooses can extract information about within-group conflicts, and the identity of at least some protagonists, from vocal cues alone.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the playback experiments showing differential responses.

claims.claim: Male little blue penguins had an increased heartrate after hearing vocalisations produced by winners of a contest compared to those produced by losers.
claims.source: This adds to a growing body of work demonstrating the ability of social species to garner information acoustically about aggressive interactions (Gouzoules et al., 1984; Slocombe et al., 2010; Slocombe and Zuberbühler, 2007); for example, male little blue penguins had an increased heartrate after hearing vocalisations produced by winners of a contest compared to those produced by losers (Mouterde et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Acoustic monitoring is beneficial as it allows information acquisition in environments where it would be difficult to do so visually or when group members are widely scattered.
claims.source: Acoustic monitoring is beneficial as it allows information acquisition in environments where it would be difficult to do so visually (eg, in low-light and dense vegetation) or when group members are widely scattered and communication is needed over long distances (Bradbury and Vehrencamp, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature and general knowledge about acoustic communication.

claims.claim: Acoustic information can be gathered at a relatively low cost: it can be done whilst still actively foraging and at a safe distance that minimises the risk of receiving redirected aggression.
claims.source: Moreover, acoustic information can be gathered at a relatively low cost: it can be done whilst still actively foraging (Hollén et al., 2008) and, in the case of aggressive encounters, at a safe distance that minimises the risk of the information-gatherer receiving any redirected aggression.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature and logical inference.

claims.claim: Monitoring behaviours acoustically is likely not possible for all within-group interactions or in all social systems.
claims.source: Monitoring behaviours acoustically is likely not possible for all within-group interactions (eg, grooming) or in all social systems, but the calls commonly produced during and at the end of aggressive contests (Bertram et al., 2010; Slocombe et al., 2010) provide a valuable means for bystanders to inform subsequent decision-making.
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about the limitations and applicability of acoustic monitoring.

claims.claim: All subordinates might be wary of the aggressor and so potentially reduce their grooming with that individual, whereas perhaps only those who are strongly bonded to the target might engage in extra grooming with it.
claims.source: First, all subordinates might be wary of the aggressor and so potentially reduce their grooming with that individual, whereas perhaps only those who are strongly bonded to the target might engage in extra grooming with it (Fraser et al., 2009; Fraser et al., 2008); any such target-related effect might be diluted by considering all subordinates in analyses.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the differential strength of responses to aggressors versus targets.

claims.claim: There may be higher selective pressure to discriminate vocalisations from dominant individuals compared to those from other subordinates if the former are more important in terms of social relationships and status.
claims.source: Alternatively, there could be selective attention towards high-ranking individuals (Chance, 1967): there may be higher selective pressure to discriminate vocalisations from dominant individuals cf those from other subordinates if the former are more important in terms of social relationships and status.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation to the concept of selective attention.

claims.claim: In many primate species, individuals focus attention on higher-ranking groupmates or those with whom they have an antagonistic relationship, possibly to avoid aggression.
claims.source: In many primate species, for example, individuals focus attention on higher-ranking groupmates or those with whom they have an antagonistic relationship (Keverne et al., 1978; McNelis and Boatright-Horowitz, 1998), possibly to avoid aggression (Schino and Sciarretta, 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The study was conducted on Sorabi Rock Lodge, a private game reserve in the Limpopo Province, South Africa.
claims.source: We conducted our study on Sorabi Rock Lodge (24° 11′S, 30° 46′E), a private game reserve in the Limpopo Province, South Africa; full details are available in Kern and Radford, 2013.
claims.evidence: This describes the study location.

claims.claim: At the time of the study (June to October 2019; non-breeding season), eight dwarf mongoose groups (mean ± SE group size: 12.3 ± 1.7, range: 5–16) were fully habituated to the close presence of human observers on foot.
claims.source: At the time of the study (June to October 2019; non-breeding season), eight dwarf mongoose groups (mean ± SE group size: 12.3 ± 1.7, range: 5–16) were fully habituated to the close presence (<5 m) of human observers on foot.
claims.evidence: This describes the study population and timing.

claims.claim: 74.3% of 740 foraging displacement events in 12 groups involved a dominant individual as the aggressor and a subordinate individual as the target.
claims.source: We chose for the playback the combination of a dominant individual as the aggressor and a subordinate individual as a target because this is the most common dyadic pairing observed in natural foraging displacements (74.3% of 740 events in 12 groups).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observational data from the long-term study.

claims.claim: A conflict track concluded with three growls from a dominant aggressor followed by a squeal from a subordinate target.
claims.source: A conflict track concluded with three growls from a dominant aggressor followed by a squeal from a subordinate target, whilst a control track concluded with three close calls from the same dominant individual followed by one close call from the same subordinate individual as in the matched conflict track.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental stimuli, with reference to Figure 1.

claims.claim: A control track concluded with three close calls from the same dominant individual followed by one close call from the same subordinate individual as in the matched conflict track.
claims.source: A conflict track concluded with three growls from a dominant aggressor followed by a squeal from a subordinate target, whilst a control track concluded with three close calls from the same dominant individual followed by one close call from the same subordinate individual as in the matched conflict track.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental stimuli, with reference to Figure 1.

results.result: Bystanders respond to foraging displacement vocalizations with increased vigilance. Both natural foraging displacements (C38) and playback-simulated displacements (C39) resulted in significantly increased vigilance in focal foragers compared to control conditions, demonstrating that vocal cues alone are sufficient to trigger this response (C40, C41).
results.evaluation: Claims C38 and C39 provide statistically significant evidence (p<0.001 for both) from matched observational and experimental designs with appropriate sample sizes (N=16 and N=17). The use of both natural observations and playback experiments strengthens the conclusion that vocal cues are sufficient. The experimental design with matched controls is appropriate.

results.result: Dwarf mongoose bystanders do not engage in immediate post-conflict affiliative behavior. No grooming occurred in the 5 minutes following either natural or simulated foraging displacements (C42), leading to the conclusion that bystanders do not engage in immediate post-conflict affiliation (C44). This is contextualized by the fact that grooming is rare during foraging periods (C43).
results.evaluation: Claims C42 and C44 are supported by clear observational and experimental data showing absence of grooming in the immediate aftermath. However, the interpretation is somewhat limited by the baseline rarity of grooming during foraging (C43), which makes it difficult to distinguish between active avoidance and normal behavior. The conclusion is reasonable but could benefit from additional controls.

results.result: Fewer individuals participated in grooming on evenings following simulated conflict afternoons. Group members were significantly less likely to be involved in grooming interactions following conflict afternoons compared to control afternoons (GLMM: χ²=5.401, p=0.020, N=8 groups).
results.evaluation: Claim C48 provides statistically significant evidence with appropriate mixed-model analysis accounting for repeated measures and group structure. The sample size of 8 groups is modest but adequate for this type of field study. The p-value meets the conventional significance threshold.

results.result: Individuals that did groom after conflict afternoons groomed more intensively than on control evenings. Those individuals that engaged in grooming spent significantly more time grooming (C49: χ²=15.873, p<0.001), groomed more frequently (C50: χ²=8.010, p=0.005), and had longer grooming bouts (C51: χ²=3.958, p=0.047) on conflict evenings compared to controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 provide converging statistical evidence from multiple measures (proportion of time, frequency, bout duration) all showing consistent directional effects. The statistical analyses appropriately use mixed models with nested random effects. All three measures reach statistical significance, providing robust support for increased grooming intensity among participants.

results.result: Subordinate bystanders reduced grooming with simulated aggressors on conflict evenings. Subordinates groomed less with the dominant pair overall (C55: Z=2.240, p=0.021), and this was specifically driven by reduced grooming with the simulated aggressor in terms of both proportion of time (C56: Z=2.521, p=0.008) and proportion of subordinates participating (C57: Z=2.201, p=0.033).
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C57 provide statistically significant evidence with appropriate non-parametric tests. The specificity of the effect (reduced grooming with simulated aggressor but not with non-playback dominant, C58-C59) strengthens the interpretation that mongooses discriminate individual identity from vocalizations and adjust behavior accordingly. Sample size of N=8 groups is modest but adequate.

results.result: Subordinate bystanders increased grooming bout duration with one another on conflict evenings. While there was no significant difference in the proportion of time subordinates spent grooming with each other (C61: Z=1.540, p=0.146), subordinate-subordinate grooming bouts were significantly longer on conflict evenings (C60: Z=2.366, p=0.015, N=7).
results.evaluation: Claim C60 provides statistically significant evidence for increased bout duration. However, the lack of effect on total proportion of time (C61) suggests the effect is modest. The sample size dropped to N=7 for the bout duration analysis, which is small but the effect is still significant. The result is supported but represents a more subtle behavioral change than the aggressor-avoidance effect.

results.result: Subordinates did not alter grooming with the non-playback dominant. There was no treatment difference in grooming with the dominant whose calls were not played back, either in proportion of time (C58: Z=0.105, p=1.0) or proportion of subordinates participating (C59: Z=0.813, p=0.499).
results.evaluation: Claims C58 and C59 provide important negative controls showing specificity of the behavioral response. The non-significant results with appropriate statistical tests (p>0.05) support the interpretation that mongooses discriminate between individuals based on vocal cues. This strengthens the overall experimental conclusions.

results.result: Dwarf mongooses acoustically obtain, retain, and use information about within-group conflicts with temporal delay. The experimental evidence demonstrates that mongooses extract information about conflicts and protagonist identity from vocal cues (C9, C78), retain this information for 30-60 minutes (C10, C46), and use it to inform delayed conflict-management decisions (C11, C72). The specificity of responses to simulated aggressors versus non-playback dominants suggests active decision-making rather than general physiological effects (C73).
results.evaluation: This overarching conclusion is well-supported by the convergence of multiple experimental results (C48-C60) showing specific, delayed behavioral changes following playback simulations. The temporal delay (mean 37±5 min, C46) and specificity of responses provide strong evidence for memory and decision-making. The use of playback experiments (C74) appropriately isolates the role of acoustic information.

results.result: This study provides the first evidence for delayed post-conflict management behavior. The authors claim no previous studies have investigated delayed post-conflict management (C2, C18), and that the reduction in grooming of aggressors by bystanders is the first evidence for this type of delayed response (C64).
results.evaluation: Claims C2 and C18 are statements about the literature that cannot be fully verified without comprehensive literature review. Claim C64 is qualified with 'to our knowledge,' acknowledging uncertainty. While the authors cite relevant prior work (C19-C23) on delayed social memory, the specific claim of novelty for delayed post-conflict management requires acceptance of the authors' literature assessment.

results.result: Individual identity can be determined from dwarf mongoose vocalizations. The authors cite previous work demonstrating individual discrimination from close calls (C52), recruitment calls (C53), and surveillance calls (C54).
results.evaluation: These claims are supported by citations to previous literature (Sharpe et al., 2013; Kern and Radford, 2016, 2018). The current study's results (differential responses to simulated aggressors vs. non-playback dominants) provide additional indirect support for individual vocal discrimination, though this was not directly tested here.

results.result: Study population and experimental parameters. The study was conducted on eight habituated dwarf mongoose groups (C86, C87) during the non-breeding season. Natural foraging displacements occur at 2.6±0.2 events per 3-hour session (C37), with 74.3% involving dominant aggressors and subordinate targets (C88). Experiment 2 involved 8.5±0.2 playbacks per trial (C45) with a mean delay of 37±5 minutes before grooming observations (C46). Most grooming (90%) occurs at sleeping refuges (C47).
results.evaluation: These methodological and descriptive claims are supported by observational data collected during the study. The sample sizes and parameters are clearly reported. Claim C47 cites previous work (Kern and Radford, 2018) for the 90% figure, providing appropriate context for the experimental design.

results.result: Experimental playback stimuli design. Conflict tracks contained three growls from a dominant followed by one squeal from a subordinate (C89), while control tracks contained three close calls from the same dominant followed by one close call from the same subordinate (C90).
results.evaluation: These claims describe the experimental stimuli and are supported by the methods description and Figure 1. The design appropriately controls for the number of vocalizations and individual identity while manipulating call type (conflict vs. non-conflict vocalizations).

results.result: Increased subordinate-subordinate grooming may reduce group-wide social anxiety. The increase in subordinate-subordinate grooming bout duration is consistent with bystander-bystander grooming in other species (C62), and such affiliation could reduce conflict-induced social anxiety (C63).
results.evaluation: Claim C62 appropriately compares findings to previous literature. However, C63 is speculative about the function of the behavior. While the speculation is reasonable and supported by citations, the current study did not measure stress or anxiety, so the functional interpretation remains uncertain.

results.result: Subordinates may avoid aggressors to reduce redirected aggression risk. The reduced grooming with aggressors could function to avoid redirected aggression (C67), paralleling avoidance strategies in meerkats and rooks (C68).
results.evaluation: Claim C67 is speculative about the function of the observed avoidance behavior. While the comparison to other species (C68) is appropriate and supported by citations, the current study did not test whether redirected aggression actually occurs or whether avoidance reduces this risk. The functional interpretation is plausible but not directly tested.

results.result: Possible explanations for differential responses to aggressors versus targets. The stronger response to aggressors could be because all subordinates are wary of aggressors while only bonded individuals console targets (C83), or because there is selective attention to high-ranking individuals (C84, C85).
results.evaluation: These claims (C83-C84) are explicitly speculative explanations for patterns in the data. While the speculations are reasonable and C85 is supported by citations to primate literature, these alternative explanations were not tested in the current study. The authors appropriately present these as possibilities rather than conclusions.

results.result: Playback design isolates bystander-driven effects. The use of playback simulations means delayed grooming effects are most likely driven by subordinate bystanders behaving differently toward perceived protagonists, rather than by protagonist behavior.
results.evaluation: Claim C74 is a reasonable inference about the experimental design. Since the 'protagonists' did not actually engage in conflict and were unaware of the playbacks, any changes in grooming patterns must be driven by bystander perceptions and decisions. This is a strength of the playback approach, though it's possible protagonists could detect and respond to altered bystander behavior.

results.result: Background on post-conflict behavior in animals. Within-group conflict can be costly (C12) and conflict-management strategies have evolved (C13). Previous research has documented reconciliation (C14), wariness (C15), and bystander-initiated affiliation with victims (C16) or aggressors (C17) in the immediate aftermath of conflicts.
results.evaluation: These claims summarize established knowledge from the literature and are appropriately supported by citations. They provide necessary context for the current study but do not represent new findings.

results.result: Animals can remember past social events and use them in later decisions. Previous experimental evidence shows that various species (baboons C20, vervet monkeys C21, chimpanzees C22, wasps C23) can remember past events and use this information in later social decisions (C19), though this is cognitively challenging (C24).
results.evaluation: These claims appropriately summarize relevant prior work and are supported by citations. They establish the broader context of delayed social memory and decision-making, providing justification for investigating delayed post-conflict behavior.

results.result: Vocalizations provide information about within-group conflicts. Many species vocalize during contests (C25, C26, C27), and these vocalizations likely provide bystanders with information about conflict occurrence, participants, and outcomes (C28).
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C27 are supported by citations to previous literature. Claim C28 involves some inference about function ('likely provide') but is reasonable given the cited literature and is supported by the current study's findings.

results.result: Background on dwarf mongoose social behavior. Dwarf mongooses live in cooperatively breeding groups (C29) where grooming is the main affiliative behavior (C30) that underpins relationships (C31), increases after stress (C32), and is traded for cooperation (C33). Within-group aggression includes targeted aggression (C34) and foraging displacements (C35, C36).
results.evaluation: These claims provide essential background on the study species and are supported by citations to previous literature. They establish the ecological and social context necessary for interpreting the experimental results.

results.result: Previous studies show mixed results for bystander-aggressor grooming. Some studies documented increased grooming of aggressors by bystanders immediately after contests (C65), while others found no such increase (C66).
results.evaluation: These claims appropriately summarize previous literature showing inconsistent findings, providing context for why the current study's finding of reduced grooming with aggressors is notable. The claims are supported by appropriate citations.

results.result: Within-group conflict has wide-reaching effects on social relationships. The results support that conflict affects interactions beyond protagonists (C69), that bystanders employ different strategies depending on participant identity (C70), and that disagreements have varied implications for affiliative behavior and social structure (C71).
results.evaluation: These claims are reasonable conclusions drawn from the experimental results (C48-C60) and appropriately contextualized with citations to previous work. They represent valid generalizations from the specific findings.

results.result: Broader implications for social cognition. Previous work showed mongooses can use vocal information to reward cooperative contributions (C75). The current findings support that mongooses and other social species constantly monitor groupmates and use memories to inform decisions (C76), consistent with social intelligence hypotheses (C77).
results.evaluation: Claim C75 appropriately cites previous work. Claims C76 and C77 are reasonable generalizations from the current findings, appropriately contextualized with citations. These represent valid broader implications of the specific experimental results.

results.result: Benefits and limitations of acoustic monitoring. Acoustic monitoring allows information acquisition in challenging visual environments or when individuals are scattered (C80), can be done while foraging and at safe distances (C81), though it's not possible for all interactions or social systems (C82). Previous work shows other species also extract information from contest vocalizations (C79).
results.evaluation: These claims appropriately discuss the advantages and limitations of acoustic communication for social monitoring. Claims C80-C81 are supported by citations and logical reasoning. Claim C82 appropriately acknowledges limitations. Claim C79 provides relevant comparative context.

results.result: Bystanders show increased vigilance following foraging displacements in dwarf mongooses. Both natural observations and playback experiments demonstrated that focal foragers spent significantly more time vigilant after conflict events compared to control situations, indicating that vocal cues alone are sufficient to trigger this response.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 requests 'a little more information on why vigilance was measured' and asks 'Does vigilance indicate being wary of conspecifics? How could you tease apart vigilance for predators versus that for conspecifics?' The reviewer also notes that 'the increased vigilance result is comparatively neglected in the discussion,' suggesting the interpretation and biological significance of this finding needs clarification. The editors additionally request evaluation of 'effects of increased vigilance on foraging success (satiation)' to support conclusions, or acknowledgment if such analyses are impractical.

results.result: Bystanders do not engage in immediate post-conflict affiliative behavior following foraging displacements. No grooming was observed in the 5 minutes following either natural or simulated foraging displacements, leading to the conclusion that dwarf mongoose bystanders do not engage in post-conflict affiliative behavior immediately after hearing within-group contests.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 questions why grooming was measured during foraging in Experiment 1 'when it was noted that mongooses rarely groom in this context,' suggesting the null result may be confounded by the behavioral context rather than representing a true absence of immediate post-conflict affiliation. This raises uncertainty about whether the lack of grooming reflects genuine absence of immediate conflict management or simply inappropriate measurement timing.

results.result: Delayed grooming patterns show complex changes following simulated conflict. Fewer individuals groomed on conflict evenings compared to control evenings, but those that did groom spent significantly more time grooming, grooming more frequently and for longer per bout after simulated increases in conflict.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises concerns about the statistical modeling framework, stating 'The modelling framework used to analyse the proportion of time grooming and the rate of grooming in linear models is not the most appropriate given the distribution of the data' and recommends using β error distributions for proportion data and Poisson models for rate data. Reviewer 2 also notes that 'the use of language like "strong" and "compelling" evidence is a little overstated given the small sample sizes' and requests that means ± SE be included for easier evaluation of effect strength. These methodological concerns create uncertainty about the robustness of the findings.

results.result: Subordinates showed identity-specific grooming avoidance of simulated aggressors. Following conflict trials, subordinates groomed significantly less with the simulated aggressor (both in proportion of time and proportion of subordinates participating) but showed no treatment difference in grooming with the non-playback dominant, demonstrating discrimination of protagonist identity.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises a critical concern about experimental validity, asking 'Was the aggressor/victim in earshot when the playback of their calls was made (experiment 2)?' and requests more convincing evidence 'that hearing an interaction that does not match what an individual sees, or hearing yourself in an interaction you know you weren't involved in, does not change the behaviour of bystanders or simulated aggressors/victims.' This concern about potential confounding effects of the playback design creates uncertainty about whether the observed grooming patterns truly reflect memory-based decision-making or could be influenced by the experimental manipulation itself.

results.result: Subordinate-subordinate grooming bouts were significantly longer on conflict evenings compared to control evenings, though there was no significant difference in the overall proportion of time spent grooming between subordinates. This increase in bout duration parallels bystander-bystander grooming increases seen in other species immediately after contests.
results.evaluation: While Reviewer 2 raises general statistical concerns about the modeling framework for proportion and rate data, no specific critique is directed at this subordinate-subordinate grooming finding. The reviewers accept this as part of the overall pattern showing that 'bystanders can employ different conflict-management strategies depending on the identity of the group members involved,' as noted in the acceptance summary.

results.result: Dwarf mongooses demonstrate delayed post-conflict management through acoustic information processing. The study provides evidence that mongooses acoustically obtain information about within-group contests including protagonist identity, retain that information for 30-60 minutes, and use it to inform conflict-management decisions with a temporal delay, as shown by changes in evening grooming patterns following afternoon playbacks.
results.evaluation: The editors note that 'the temporal scale mentioned in the abstract and introduction is somewhat unclear – what exactly is the "delay" and what is its biological significance/justification?' They specifically ask 'what is known about physiological stress responses in this species (e.g., peak response and recovery time)?' This indicates that while the delayed response is documented, its biological interpretation and significance remain unclear. Additionally, Reviewer 2's concerns about statistical methods and experimental design (hearing playbacks of one's own calls) affect confidence in the mechanistic interpretation.

results.result: The use of playback simulations means delayed grooming effects are most likely driven by subordinate bystanders behaving differently towards perceived protagonists, rather than solicitation or rejection of grooming by the protagonists themselves.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 directly challenges this interpretation by asking whether 'the aggressor/victim in earshot when the playback of their calls was made' and requesting more convincing evidence that the playback design doesn't confound the results. The reviewer's concern that individuals might hear themselves in interactions they weren't actually involved in undermines confidence in attributing the effects solely to bystander decision-making.

results.result: This study represents the first investigation of delayed post-conflict management behavior and the first evidence for later reduction in grooming of aggressors by bystanders, contrasting with previous studies that documented either increased or no change in immediate bystander-aggressor grooming.
results.evaluation: The acceptance summary explicitly states this work 'expands our understanding of social dynamics in group-living species by providing evidence that bystanders of within-group conflict may play a role in maintaining group cohesion' and provides 'a valuable contribution, and contrast, to existing work in this field.' Reviewer 1 notes 'these statements are really important to highlight the significance of your findings' regarding the novelty claims, though suggests spending more time discussing them.

results.result: Within-group conflict affects interactions beyond those between protagonists, with bystanders employing different conflict-management strategies depending on the identity of group members involved. These disagreements between individuals have wide-reaching implications for affiliative behavior that underpins dyadic relationships and social structure.
results.evaluation: The acceptance summary explicitly endorses this conclusion, stating the study 'expands our understanding of social dynamics in group-living species by providing evidence that bystanders of within-group conflict may play a role in maintaining group cohesion.' Reviewer 1 affirms 'the research is meaningful' and presents 'unique results of interest to those studying social species,' though suggests improving 'overall cohesion of information presented.'

results.result: Mongooses and other social species constantly monitor groupmate behavior and interactions, using memories to inform later decisions. The cognitive demands of tracking individuals and their behaviors, remembering information, and using it for decision-making explain why social interactions are believed to be strong drivers of animal intelligence.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 expresses concern that 'this statement about cognitive ability and intelligence comes somewhat out of the blue and may not be the best statement to end your article' unless 'the link between post-conflict behaviour and social animal intelligence is discussed prior.' This suggests the cognitive/intelligence framing needs better integration and justification within the manuscript's narrative.

comparisons.comparison: Both address claims C3, C38-C41 about vocal cues and vigilance. OpenEval finds the evidence statistically significant and well-designed (SUPPORTED), while peer reviewers request clarification on why vigilance was measured, how to distinguish predator vs. conspecific vigilance, and note the finding is neglected in discussion (UNCERTAIN). Disagreement on interpretation and completeness of the vigilance findings.

Both address claims C4, C42, C44 about absence of immediate grooming. OpenEval acknowledges baseline rarity limitation but finds conclusion reasonable (SUPPORTED), while peer reviewers question measuring grooming during foraging when it's rare in that context, suggesting the null result may be confounded by behavioral context (UNCERTAIN). Peer review raises more fundamental concerns about measurement validity.

OpenEval addresses C5, C48 about increased vigilance with appropriate statistical analysis (SUPPORTED). Peer R3 addresses C5, C6, C48-C51 about both vigilance and grooming patterns, raising concerns about statistical modeling framework (recommending β distributions for proportions, Poisson for rates) and questioning use of 'strong' and 'compelling' language given small sample sizes (UNCERTAIN). Peer review has broader scope and methodological concerns.

OpenEval addresses C6, C49-C51 about increased grooming intensity with converging evidence from multiple measures (SUPPORTED). Peer R3 includes these claims (C6, C49-C51) along with C5, C48, raising statistical modeling concerns about the analytical framework for proportion and rate data (UNCERTAIN). Overlapping claims but peer review questions methodological appropriateness.

Both address claims C7, C55-C57 about reduced grooming with simulated aggressors. OpenEval finds the specificity strengthens interpretation of individual discrimination (SUPPORTED). Peer R4 also includes C58-C59 and raises critical concerns about experimental validity: whether aggressors/victims heard their own playback calls and whether this confounds the results (UNCERTAIN). Fundamental disagreement on experimental design validity.

OpenEval addresses C58-C59 as important negative controls showing specificity (SUPPORTED). Peer R4 addresses C7, C55-C59 together, questioning whether hearing one's own calls in playback confounds the interpretation of memory-based decision-making (UNCERTAIN). Peer review challenges the experimental design that OpenEval accepts.

Both address claims C8, C60-C61 about subordinate-subordinate grooming. OpenEval finds evidence supported despite modest effect (SUPPORTED). Peer R5 also includes C62 and notes no specific critique of this finding, accepting it as part of the overall pattern (SUPPORTED). Agreement on this specific finding, though peer review has general statistical concerns elsewhere.

OpenEval addresses C62-C63 about functional interpretation of grooming patterns, finding C63 speculative since stress wasn't measured (UNCERTAIN). Peer R5 addresses C8, C60-C62 and supports the subordinate-subordinate grooming finding without specific critique (SUPPORTED). Limited overlap on C62; different evaluation focus.

Both address claims C9-C11, C72-C73, C78 about delayed post-conflict management and memory-based decision-making. OpenEval finds the conclusion well-supported by convergent evidence (SUPPORTED). Peer reviewers question the temporal scale's biological significance, ask about physiological stress responses, and note concerns about statistical methods and experimental design affect confidence in mechanistic interpretation (UNCERTAIN). Both address claim C74 about bystander-driven effects. OpenEval finds this a reasonable inference and strength of the playback approach (SUPPORTED). Peer reviewers directly challenge this by questioning whether aggressors/victims heard their own playback calls, undermining confidence in attributing effects solely to bystander decision-making (UNCERTAIN).
